rationale: Kings preserves Hezekiah's plea for peace in his days after the threat of Babylonian loss; Chronicles explicitly states that wrath was deferred following his and Jerusalem's humbling.

The public covenant reading follows the law's principle that assembled Israel hear and learn its words; the law's context specifies the Feast of Tents, whereas Chronicles describes Josiah's covenant assembly.
David's recorded arrangement of Levites by ancestral houses supplies the specific institutional background for the Levite preparation Josiah orders by David's writing.
Hezekiah's Passover likewise assigns slaughter to Levites and blood handling to priests, supplying a specific earlier example of the cooperation in Josiah's Passover.
Both describe Nebuchadnezzar gaining power over Judah's king; Chronicles specifies the king's fetters and removal to Babylon, while Daniel also emphasizes the captured temple vessels.

Jeremiah names Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim and announces his removal into Chaldean hands, supplying the prophetic judgment background to this brief condemned reign; the age and reign length are supplied by Chronicles.
Ezra opens with the same first-year setting, fulfillment of Jeremiah's word, divine stirring of Cyrus, and written kingdom-wide proclamation.
Ezra preserves Cyrus's acknowledgment of the God of heaven, commission to build the Jerusalem temple, and invitation for God's people to go up, continuing the proclamation that closes Chronicles.
